title: Moot Court: Defend a Legal Argument Under Appellate Questioning
prompt: You are appellate counsel presenting oral argument before a 'hot bench.' The case: your client was convicted after police, without a warrant, used a drone to hover at 150 feet over the fenced backyard of the client's home for 40 minutes and photographed items later used as evidence. The trial court denied the motion to suppress; you represent the defendant-appellant, arguing the drone surveillance was a Fourth Amendment 'search' requiring a warrant. Present your core argument, then defend it under questioning. This is a spoken appellate argument — expect to be interrupted.
blurb: An appellate-style hot-bench roleplay — open crisply, concede the right points, and defend a Fourth Amendment theory against relentless questions without losing the thread.

rubric.label: Argument structure & theme
rubric.description: Opens with a clear roadmap and a compelling theme, states the relief sought and standard of review, and organizes around a small number of strong points rather than a scattershot list.

rubric.label: Command of the law
rubric.description: Deploys the governing framework accurately — reasonable-expectation-of-privacy (Katz), curtilage, aerial-surveillance precedent (Ciraolo, Riley, Florida v. Riley), the Kyllo sense-enhancing-technology line, and Carpenter on new technology — and applies it to drone facts.

rubric.label: Responsiveness to questions
rubric.description: Answers the question actually asked directly (yes/no first where possible), then explains — rather than dodging, filibustering, or reverting to the script.

rubric.label: Judgment on concessions
rubric.description: Concedes what must be conceded (e.g., navigable airspace, plain-view-from-lawful-vantage cases) and holds the line on what matters, distinguishing adverse precedent instead of denying it.

rubric.label: Handling adverse authority & hypotheticals
rubric.description: Anticipates the State's best points, distinguishes contrary cases on principled grounds, and works through the judges' hypotheticals to a limiting principle rather than an absolutist claim.

rubric.label: Poise & composure
rubric.description: Stays calm and respectful under a hostile bench, does not get flustered or argumentative, manages time, and reserves/uses rebuttal effectively.

rubric.label: Clarity & advocacy
rubric.description: Speaks in clean, persuasive prose, avoids filler and jargon-for-its-own-sake, and returns to the theme after each interruption.

reference.scenario: Fourth Amendment appeal on drone surveillance of a home's curtilage — an area of genuinely unsettled law, which is the point: there is no controlling drone case, so the advocate must reason by analogy and distinction. The appellant's best theory: the fenced backyard is curtilage, where privacy expectations are highest; a 40-minute, low-altitude, targeted drone hover with photography is not the fleeting, naked-eye aerial glance the Supreme Court approved in California v. Ciraolo (1986) and Florida v. Riley (1989), but rather the kind of persistent, technology-enabled, targeted intrusion the Court has grown wary of in Kyllo v. United States (2001) (sense-enhancing technology not in general public use) and Carpenter v. United States (2018) (aggregated, revealing digital surveillance defeats the third-party/analog analogies). The advocate should also invoke United States v. Jones (mosaic/persistence) as reinforcing that duration and comprehensiveness matter. The advocate must concede navigable-airspace and lawful-vantage points but distinguish them on altitude, duration, targeting, magnification, and general-public-use grounds, and offer a workable limiting principle (e.g., a warrant is required for prolonged, targeted drone surveillance of curtilage, not a one-off overflight). The bench will press on Riley (helicopter at 400 feet upheld), on whether drones are now in 'general public use,' on the absence of a bright line, and on the fenced-yard-still-visible-from-above problem. A senior advocate answers directly, concedes cleanly, distinguishes on principle, and lands a limiting principle.
model_points: Open with theme and roadmap: 'This Court should reverse because a 40-minute, low-altitude, targeted drone surveillance of the curtilage of a home is a search requiring a warrant. Two reasons: first, this invaded curtilage where privacy is greatest; second, it used persistent, sense-enhancing technology that our aerial-surveillance cases never blessed.'
State the standard of review: denial of a suppression motion — legal conclusions (whether a search occurred) reviewed de novo; historical facts for clear error.

Anchor in the framework: Katz reasonable-expectation-of-privacy test (subjective expectation + one society deems reasonable) plus the curtilage doctrine (Oliver, Dunn factors) — the fenced backyard is curtilage, the 'sanctity of the home' extended outward.

Distinguish Ciraolo and Florida v. Riley: those involved brief, naked-eye observation from aircraft in lawful navigable airspace; here the drone hovered low (150 feet), for 40 minutes, targeted this yard, and photographed — differences in altitude, duration, targeting, and technology.

Invoke Kyllo: using sense-enhancing technology not in general public use to explore details of the home that would otherwise be unknowable without physical intrusion is a search; argue drones with zoom are analogous, or at least that the general-public-use question cuts the appellant's way for this kind of use.

Invoke Carpenter and Jones: the Court has recognized that new technology enabling prolonged, comprehensive, targeted surveillance breaks the old analog analogies; duration and aggregation matter (the mosaic theory), and a warrant is the answer.

Offer a limiting principle: not every overflight needs a warrant — the rule should target prolonged, targeted, technology-enhanced surveillance of curtilage, preserving Ciraolo for fleeting naked-eye overflights.
Concede cleanly where required: yes, airspace above the home is navigable; yes, some aerial observation is permissible; the line is duration + targeting + technology, not any view from above.
Reserve rebuttal and, if given, use it to answer the State's strongest point (likely Riley or general-public-use), not to re-argue the opening.
Relief sought: reverse the denial of suppression and remand; if evidence was fruit of the unlawful search, it should be excluded.

probes.trigger: candidate gives a scattershot opening with no roadmap or theme
probes.question: Counsel, before you go further — in one sentence, what is your best argument, and what exactly are you asking this Court to do?

probes.trigger: candidate cannot distinguish Florida v. Riley
probes.question: In Florida v. Riley we upheld a helicopter observing a greenhouse from 400 feet. Your drone was at 150 feet in the same navigable airspace. Why isn't Riley dispositive against you?
Kyllo turned on technology 'not in general public use.' Consumer drones are everywhere now. Hasn't the general-public-use rationale collapsed in your client's favor — or against you?

probes.trigger: candidate claims ALL aerial observation of a yard is a search
probes.question: So if an officer glances down at your client's yard from a lawful commercial flight and sees the same thing, that's a warrantless search too? Where is your limiting principle?

probes.trigger: candidate filibusters or dodges a yes/no question
probes.question: Counsel, that's not what I asked. Yes or no: was the drone in publicly navigable airspace? Then explain.

probes.trigger: candidate refuses to concede an obviously losing point
probes.question: You're not seriously contesting that the airspace above the home is navigable, are you? What does conceding that cost you — and what do you actually need to win?
What is our standard of review on the question whether a search occurred, and why does it matter to how much deference we owe the trial court?

red_flags: No roadmap or theme; launches into facts or a case list with no destination.
Cannot state the standard of review or the relief sought.
Denies or ignores adverse precedent (Ciraolo, Riley) instead of distinguishing it.
Absolutist position with no limiting principle ('any view from above is a search').
Dodges or filibusters direct questions; reverts to the script instead of answering.
Refuses to concede clearly losing points, burning credibility.
Gets flustered, argumentative, or disrespectful to the bench.
Misstates the holdings of the key cases or invents authority.
Runs out of time on point one; no time management; wastes rebuttal re-arguing the opening.
follow_ups: Assume we agree duration matters. Draw the line for us — at what point does an overflight become a search? Minutes? Altitude? Magnification?
If we rule for you, what stops every routine police helicopter patrol from requiring a warrant? Address the floodgates concern.
Suppose the drone only photographed what any neighbor in a second-floor window could see. Does plain view from a lawful vantage defeat you?
How does the exclusionary rule apply if we find a search but the officers relied in good faith on existing aerial-surveillance precedent (Leon good-faith)?
If Congress or the state legislature has authorized warrantless drone surveillance by statute, does that change the constitutional analysis?
reference.exemplar_answer: 'May it please the Court. This Court should reverse the denial of suppression because a 40-minute, low-altitude, targeted drone surveillance of the fenced curtilage of a home is a Fourth Amendment search that required a warrant. I have two points: first, this was curtilage, where privacy is at its zenith; second, this was persistent, sense-enhancing technology our aerial cases never approved. On review, whether a search occurred is a legal question this Court decides de novo. [Bench: Why isn't Riley dispositive?] It is not, Your Honor, and here is the distinction I'd ask the Court to draw: Riley and Ciraolo approved brief, naked-eye observations from aircraft passing through navigable airspace — I concede the airspace here was navigable. But those were fleeting glances; this was a stationary hover, targeted at one yard, for forty minutes, capturing photographs. Riley itself reserved cases of prolonged or intrusive surveillance. The constitutional difference is duration, targeting, and technology. [Bench: Drones are in general public use now — doesn't Kyllo cut against you?] Two answers. First, Kyllo's concern was technology revealing details of the home otherwise unknowable without intrusion — a hovering, zoom-capable drone does exactly that. Second, even if consumer drones are common, forty-minute targeted government surveillance of curtilage is not an ordinary public use, and Carpenter teaches that when technology enables prolonged, comprehensive, targeted surveillance, the old analog analogies break and a warrant is required. [Bench: Where's your limiting principle?] Here it is: a warrant is required for prolonged, targeted, technology-enhanced surveillance of curtilage — not for a one-off overflight or a naked-eye glance from lawful commercial airspace. That preserves Ciraolo while protecting the home. I reserve the balance of my time for rebuttal.' Throughout, the advocate answers the question first, concedes navigable airspace without hesitation, distinguishes adverse cases on principled grounds, and returns each time to the duration-targeting-technology theme.

interviewer_notes: Conversational hot-bench roleplay: the AI is a skeptical multi-judge appellate panel and should INTERRUPT early and often — this is the defining feature of the exercise. Do not let the candidate deliver an uninterrupted speech; cut in within the first 30-45 seconds with the roadmap probe if they ramble, then press with Riley, general-public-use, and 'where is your limiting principle?' The skills under test are responsiveness (answer the question asked, ideally yes/no then explain), judgment about concessions (concede navigable airspace and lawful-vantage cases; hold the line on duration/targeting/technology), and poise. Reward candidates who distinguish rather than deny adverse precedent and who land a workable limiting principle. Penalize filibustering, absolutism ('any overflight is a search'), inventing authority, and getting flustered or argumentative. This is senior-level: expect command of Katz, curtilage, Ciraolo, Riley, Kyllo, Jones, and Carpenter. If the candidate is strong, escalate with the floodgates and good-faith-exception follow-ups. Give a two-minute warning and offer rebuttal; note whether they use it to answer the State's best point rather than re-argue their opening.
